stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Solvang's finding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Most songbirds that breed in northern Europe migrate south each autumn along a single, consistent route.
• In 2022, ornithologist Henrik Solvang attached lightweight trackers to 30 garden warblers nesting near Trondheim, Norway.
• Solvang found that individual warblers used different routes in different years, sometimes shifting by more than 400 kilometers.
• Such route flexibility had previously been documented only in large birds, such as geese and storks.
choices: In 2022, Solvang attached lightweight trackers to 30 garden warblers that were nesting near Trondheim, Norway.
Solvang's garden warblers changed migration routes between years, a flexibility previously documented only in large birds.
Most songbirds that breed in northern Europe migrate south each autumn along a single, consistent route.
Some of the garden warblers that Solvang tracked shifted their migration routes by more than 400 kilometers.
explanation: The goal asks why Solvang's finding matters. The last note says why: this kind of flexibility had been seen only in large birds before. Choice B states the finding and includes that comparison, so you can see what makes it significant.

A.why: You picked a description of the study's method: who, how many birds, where. It never says what Solvang found or why that finding matters.

C.why: You picked the background note. It sets up a contrast but never mentions Solvang's finding, so it can't show that finding's significance.

D.why: You picked a striking fact without the comparison that makes it significant. A 400-kilometer shift matters only because such flexibility was previously known only in large birds, and this choice leaves that out.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the achievement of the county's program in reducing childhood lead poisoning. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Kestrel County once had one of the highest childhood lead-poisoning rates in its state.
• In 2016, county health officials began offering free home inspections and lead pipe replacements.
• By 2023, more than 9,000 homes had been inspected through the program.
• Over that period, the county's childhood lead-poisoning rate fell by 78 percent, the largest decline recorded in the state.
choices: Kestrel County once had one of the highest childhood lead-poisoning rates of any county in its state.
By 2023, the county's program had provided free lead inspections for more than 9,000 homes.
Kestrel County's program of free inspections and pipe replacements eliminated childhood lead poisoning statewide.
Under the county's program, childhood lead poisoning fell 78 percent, the largest decline recorded in the state.
explanation: The goal is the program's achievement in reducing lead poisoning, so the answer has to give the health outcome. Choice D gives the 78 percent drop and adds that it was the state's largest decline, which shows how big the achievement was.

A.why: You picked the background problem. It describes the situation before the program and says nothing about what the program achieved.

B.why: You confused the program's activity with its outcome. Inspecting 9,000 homes is what the program did. The goal asks what it achieved in reducing lead poisoning, and this choice never mentions lead-poisoning rates.

C.why: You accepted an exaggeration. The notes describe a 78 percent drop in one county, not the elimination of lead poisoning across the whole state.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Natarajan's finding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• By the 1990s, invasive rats on Calder Island had nearly eliminated the island's ground-nesting seabirds.
• Conservationists removed all rats from the island in 2009.
• Within ten years, nesting seabirds rose from 40 pairs to over 2,000.
• Ecologist Priya Natarajan found that guano from the returning seabirds tripled nitrogen levels in nearby coral reefs.
• This was the first documented case of rat removal benefiting an ecosystem beyond an island's shoreline.
choices: Natarajan's reef findings were the first documented case of rat removal benefiting an ecosystem beyond an island's shoreline.
After rats were removed from Calder Island in 2009, nesting seabirds rose from 40 pairs to over 2,000.
Natarajan found that guano from Calder Island's seabirds tripled nitrogen levels in nearby coral reefs.
By the 1990s, invasive rats on Calder Island had nearly eliminated the island's ground-nesting seabirds.
explanation: The goal names Natarajan's finding, and the final note explains why it matters: it was the first documented case of rat removal helping an ecosystem beyond the shoreline. Choice A is built around that 'first.'

B.why: You picked an impressive result, but it belongs to the conservationists' rat removal, not Natarajan's finding. The goal asks about the significance of Natarajan's work.

C.why: You picked an accurate description of what Natarajan found, but it never says why the finding matters. The fact that it was a first is missing.

D.why: You picked the background note. It describes the problem before any rat removal and doesn't mention Natarajan at all.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the historical significance of the Halden Street project. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1971, the city of Marrow Bay closed Halden Street, its main commercial street, to cars.
• Local merchants had opposed the plan, fearing they would lose customers who arrived by car.
• Within three years, retail sales on Halden Street rose 35 percent.
• Halden Street was one of the first pedestrian-only streets in North America.
• Dozens of cities later copied its design.
choices: In 1971, Marrow Bay closed Halden Street, its main commercial street, to cars and opened it to pedestrians.
Halden Street merchants opposed the 1971 plan, fearing they would lose customers who arrived by car.
One of North America's first pedestrian-only streets, Halden Street became a model that dozens of cities copied.
As the world's first pedestrian-only street, Halden Street raised retail sales in every city that copied it.
explanation: Historical significance means the project's place in history. Choice C says Halden Street was among North America's first pedestrian streets and that dozens of cities copied it, which together explain why it mattered beyond Marrow Bay.

A.why: You picked the event and its date. The choice says what happened in 1971 but not why it mattered historically.

B.why: You picked a detail about local opposition. It's interesting context, but it doesn't show the project's historical importance.

D.why: You accepted claims the notes don't support. The notes say 'one of the first' in North America, not the world's first. They also report higher sales only on Halden Street, not in the cities that copied it.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Wierzba's results. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many sprint coaches assume that athletes older than 35 cannot improve their top running speed.
• Physiologist Tomasz Wierzba recruited 24 masters sprinters aged 36 to 52.
• The sprinters completed a 16-week plyometric training program.
• By the end of the program, their average top speed had increased by 4 percent.
choices: Wierzba recruited 24 masters sprinters, aged 36 to 52, to complete a 16-week plyometric training program.
Many sprint coaches assume that athletes who are older than 35 cannot improve their top running speed.
Contrary to a common coaching belief, Wierzba's sprinters, all over 35, raised their top speed by 4 percent.
After a 16-week plyometric program, the masters sprinters in Wierzba's study raised their average top speed 4 percent.
explanation: The results matter because they go against the belief in the first note. Choice C sets the 4 percent gain against that coaching belief and says the sprinters were all over 35, which is what makes the result significant.

A.why: You picked the study's method. It says who took part and what they did, but it gives no result and no reason the result matters.

B.why: You picked only the background belief. Without the result that challenges it, this choice says nothing about Wierzba's results.

D.why: You picked the result without the comparison that makes it significant. A 4 percent gain matters because coaches think athletes over 35 can't get faster, and this choice leaves that out.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of HailCast-2. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hailstorms cause billions of dollars in crop damage each year.
• Most existing hail forecasts can predict hail only about 30 minutes in advance.
• In 2024, meteorologist Ana Ferreira's team tested a forecasting model called HailCast-2 across 600 storms in Argentina.
• HailCast-2 correctly predicted large hail up to three hours in advance, six times earlier than most existing forecasts.
choices: HailCast-2 predicted large hail up to three hours in advance, six times earlier than most existing forecasts.
Tested across 600 storms in Argentina, HailCast-2 correctly predicted large hail up to three hours in advance.
In 2024, Ferreira's team tested HailCast-2, a hail forecasting model, across 600 storms in Argentina.
Because hailstorms cause billions in crop damage, most forecasters choose to predict hail only 30 minutes ahead.
explanation: HailCast-2's importance is relative: three hours is impressive only next to the usual 30 minutes. Choice A keeps that comparison ('six times earlier than most existing forecasts'), so it shows why the model matters.

B.why: You picked a bare figure without its comparison. 'Three hours' shows significance only when set against the usual 30-minute warning, and this choice leaves that out.

C.why: You picked a description of the test: who, when, where. It never says what HailCast-2 achieved or why that matters.

D.why: You accepted a causal link the notes never make. The notes don't say forecasters choose a 30-minute window because of crop damage, and this choice never mentions HailCast-2.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Okafor-Lind's finding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Vitamin B12 is found naturally almost only in animal foods.
• People on plant-based diets often need supplements to get enough B12.
• Food scientist Rui Okafor-Lind analyzed a fermented form of duckweed, a small aquatic plant.
• A 30-gram serving supplied the full daily recommended amount of B12.
• It was the first plant food shown to supply a full day's B12 in a single serving.
choices: Because vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, people on plant-based diets often need supplements.
Okafor-Lind found that a 30-gram serving of fermented duckweed contained a full day's recommended B12.
Okafor-Lind's fermented duckweed means that people on plant-based diets no longer need B12 supplements.
Okafor-Lind's fermented duckweed is the first plant food shown to supply a full day's B12 in one serving.
explanation: The last note says why the finding matters: it was a first among plant foods. Choice D states that, so it presents the result as a milestone rather than just a measurement.

A.why: You picked the background. It explains why B12 is a concern but never mentions Okafor-Lind's finding.

B.why: You picked an accurate description of the finding without its significance. The choice doesn't say that no plant food had done this before, which is the reason it matters.

C.why: You accepted a conclusion the notes never draw. One analysis of one food doesn't show that people on plant-based diets no longer need supplements.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Haldorsen's fossils. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Flowering plants were long thought to have first appeared about 130 million years ago.
• Paleobotanist Ingrid Haldorsen examined fossil leaves from a quarry in Greenland.
• The leaves have the net-like vein pattern typical of flowering plants.
• Haldorsen dated the fossils to about 165 million years ago.
• If confirmed, the fossils would push back the origin of flowering plants by about 35 million years.
choices: The fossil leaves Haldorsen examined have the net-like vein pattern that is typical of flowering plants.
Dated to 165 million years ago, Haldorsen's fossils could push back the origin of flowering plants by 35 million years.
Haldorsen dated the fossil leaves, which came from a quarry in Greenland, to about 165 million years ago.
Haldorsen's fossil leaves prove that flowering plants first evolved in Greenland 165 million years ago.
explanation: The fossils matter because they are earlier than expected. Choice B gives their age and says what it would change: the origin of flowering plants would move back 35 million years. It also keeps the notes' 'if confirmed' caution by saying 'could.'

A.why: You picked a description of what the fossils look like. The vein pattern identifies them as flowering plants but doesn't say why they matter.

C.why: You picked a bare date. '165 million years ago' is significant only next to the long-held 130-million-year estimate, and this choice leaves that comparison out.

D.why: You accepted claims stronger than the evidence. The notes say the fossils would change the timeline only if confirmed, so 'prove' goes too far. Nothing in the notes says flowering plants first evolved in Greenland.
